וכתבו לו מכאן דייקי הב"ח וסמ"ע והש"ך דהטור בעי ג"כ קנין בפניו דאל"כ לאו לכתיבה עומד וק"ק לפי מ"ש הטור כהרא"ש דהך שטרי אקנייתא אינו שטר של קנין וכמש"ל רק שכתב לו בין ילוה ובין לא ילוה ועיין מש"ל דלא קשה להרא"ש במה יקנ' דסבירא ליה לענין קנין לכ"ע עבחז"ל אם כן אין לדין זה ראי' מהמשנה כלל דכל ראי' של הרמב"ן מהא דאמרינן אין כותבין שטר למלוה בלי לוה דקשי' פשיטא וכמש"ל ומוקי לה דקאי ארישא דמיירי בקנין ולשיטת הרא"ש הא לא איירי בקנין כלל רק דאמר דמשתעבד בין ילוה או לא ילוה וא"כ פשיטא דבעי כתבו ואף דנימא מסיפא אין כותבין שטר ללוקח וכו' דשם במכירה ומתנה מודה הרא"ש דבקנין לחוד כותבין דהא תיכף ניקנה השדה ולא מצי לחזור בו כלל אפילו נתנו השטר בידו של המקנה כמ"ש הרא"ש להדיא בתשובה הנ"ל כלל ס"ו ע"ש. וכ"כ הטור לקמן ס"ס ר"נ במתנה בקנין תיכף ניקנה ועיין פרישה דכתב ג"כ בזה דבמכירה מודה הרא"ש מ"מ דוחק דמשנה כותבין שטר לעלוה ושטר למוכר יהיה בב' גווני וגם לכאורה מוכח מהרא"ש בפ' הספינה גבי זכו בשדה לפלוני וכתבו לו השטר חוזר בשטר וכו' דהקשה הרא"ש הא אמרינן לעיל סתם קנין לכתיבה עומד ותי' דמכל מקום מצי לחזור בו וקשה מה קושי' הא לשון זכו בשדה לפלוני וכתבו לו משמע דאין הפלוני לנוכח דאם לא כן הל"ל זכו בשדה לזה כנודע משפט הלשון ואם כן לאו לכתיבה עומד וכן בפ' חזקת דייק מהא דאמרינן בפ' אע"פ כתבו וחתמו והבו לי' קנו מיני' צריך לאמלוכי ודייק לאיזה צורך נאמר וכתבו הא סתם קנין לכתיבה עומד וקשה דלמא איירי שלא בפניו ומזה לכאורה משמע דהרא"ש לא סבירא ליה כרמב"ן וזהו דעת הב"י והע"ש בטור אף דכתבו לקמן סי' רל"ח בשם רמב"ן מכל מקום סבירא ליה להטור גופי' כדעת אביו אך י"ל דברי הע"ש ממה שכתב לעיל דלא בריר' ליה ודוק:
ולא יזכה המלוה עד שמ"י הלוה דין זה צל"ע כי רמ"א העתיק מדברי הטור שכתבו סי' זה ולא לחנם השמיטו רבינו המחבר כי צ"ע אם כן דאם אמר קנו ותנו אותו בידי אין למלוה זכי' בו וזהו ששנו כותבין שטר ללוה אעפ"י שאין מלוה עמו כי יאמר קנו ותנו אותו בידי וכ"כ הרא"ש להדיא בתשובה כלל ס"ו דין ג' בסוף התשובה על מ"ש הרמב"ם לוה שהשליש שטרו ולא פי' ומת דלא יתן אותו השליש ללוה דבהלואה כיון דתנן כותבין שטר ללוה אעפ"י שאין מלוה עמו חיישינן שמא לא לוה והרמב"ם מיירי בקנין דבלי קנין אין כותבין שטר בלי מלוה כנודע וא"כ הדרא קושי' המחברים על הרי"ף לדוכתי' דהא דעת הרי"ף בשטר קנין בעי מטי לידי' וראייתו מהך דמצא דייתקי קשורה על ירכו דלא יתן וטענו עליו דור שאחריו מהא דמצא שטר הקנאה בשוק יחזור דהא שעבד נפשי' ואמאי הא לא מטו לידיה ולכך פירשו דהך דייתיקי איירי במתנת ש"מ כמ"ש המחברים ועיין ריב"ש סי' קס"א שהאריך בזה ואם כן עדיין הקו' במ"ע דאיך נחזיר שטר הקנאה בלי ידיעת ורצון הלוה דילמא אמר כתבו ותנו בידי ואם כן אין למלוה זכי' בו כלל ומאתו נפל ול"ל דלא שכיח דהא אדרבא כך סדרן של לוים כותבין שטר ללוה בשאין מלוה עמו והיינו בשטרי קנין והא חששו בנפילה לדברים רבים בלתי שכיחי' הואיל ואיתרע בנפילה ומכ"ש בזה דכך שנינו כותבין שטר ללוה אע"פ שאין מלוה עמו וכך הסדר כמ"ש התו' והרא"ש בכמה דוכתי ועיין בתוס' בשמעתא דשודא דדייני בכתובות וב"ב גבי ע"א בכתב דחששו להדיא דכותבין שטר ללוה וכו' וכן אמרו בשני יב"ש דאין מוציאין זה על זה משום דכותבין שטר ללוה וכו' ע"ש סוף ב"ב ומכ"ש בזה דנפל ועוד דאם אמרינן כן נסתר קושי' שלהם על הרי"ף ולמה קמו האחרונים ובטלו דברי הראשונים והיא היא. ובאמת מדברי הטור והרא"ש אין ראי' ול"ק להו מידי דהם פי' שטרי הקנאה שכתב לו בין ילוה ובין לא ילוה ולא פי' בשטר קנין כמש"ל ואם כן שפיר אמרינן דאם אמר קנו ותנו אותו בידי אין למלוה זכי' בו עד דמטי לידי' כדעת הרי"ף וסייעתו ולא קשה כלל מהך דמצא שטר הקנאה דשם פי' אחר דהקנה בין ילוה ובין לא ילוה והא דפסק הרא"ש בהך דהיה דייתיקי קשורה דבמתנת ברי זכה המקבל לא מהך ראי' דמצא שטר הקנאה וכו' רק סברא בעלמא דקנין להקנות איך יוכל לחזור לאחר שעסוק באותו ענין ואמרו חוזר בשטר ואין חוזר בשדה כמ"ש הרא"ש בתשובה הנ"ל ולא הביא כלל ראי' מהך דמצא שטר הקנאה רק מהך דחוזר בשדה וכו' וא"ש אבל לדידן דקיי"ל כרוב מחברים דפי' שטר הקנאה היינו שטר קנין אם כן איך אפשר לומר כהנ"ל דאיך אמרינן מצא שטר הקנאה יחזיר והיא קושי' תלמידי הרי"ף ז"ל ועיין בבעה"ת שער נ"ב בסופו ותראה כדברים האלה להדיא דהך דינא תליא במחלוקת הרי"ף ודור שלאחריו דקשי' לי' מהך דמצא שטר קנין וכו' ע"ש והדבר ברור כמ"ש וכ"כ הנ"י להדיא דמ"ש רש"י בין ילוה או לא ילוה היינו קנין סתם רק סבירא ליה דקנין סתם היינו בין ילוה או לא ילוה וכ"כ יותר מפורשים עיין בא"ז ואם כן דה"ל בין ילוה או לא ילוה ולכך מותר לכתוב ללוה ש"מ דמלוה זוכה בו אף דלא ילוה לו וזה פשוט. ואמת כי גם בתשובת הרא"ש הנ"ל יש לפקפק איך פי' כרמב"ם דסבירא ליה דלכך שטר שנמצא ביד שליש לא יחזיר משום כתב ללות וכו'. הא הרמב"ם סבירא ליה בפי' שטרי אקנייתא כרי"ף ואם כן קשי' לי' מהך דמצא שטר הקנאה וכו' אך אין זה כ"כ תימא אם הרמב"ם סבירא ליה כדעת רבו הרי"ף דבעינן מטי לידו ומתרץ הך קושי' דמצא שטר אקנייתא בדחוקים רבים כמ"ש מחברים עיין אסיפת זקנים מ"ש שם. אבל לפי שהעלו האחרונים מכח הך ראי' דלא כרי"ף נסתר הנ"ל ואולי יש לומר דמה דכתב הרמ"א ולא יזכה המלוה וכו' פי' בשטר דודאי מחויב לשלם ונשתעבדו נכסים מכח קנין אבל מכל מקום השטר אין מחויב לתת לו והרי זה כמ"ש חוזר בשטר ואינו חוזר בשדה ולכך בנמצא יחזיר כיון דגוף הלואה מחויב לשלם לא חששו בנפל. אך דוחק דלא ה"ל לרמ"א לסתום כ"כ והרב בב"י בב"ה כתב על זה והכא אעפ"י שקנו מידו כיון שאמר תנו אותו בידי אינם רשאים ליתנו למלוה שלא גמר להשתעבד לו עד שילוהו ואם נתנהו למלוה מקודם שויה ליה עולה עכ"ל וכן באמת מורה לשון הטור ורמ"א ולכן צ"ע כי יפה עשה הרב מחבר שהשמיטו ועיין מ"ש עוד מזה לקמן בסי' נ"ה אי"ה. ואפשר דמ"מ מחויבים ליתן ללוה אף דנתחייב בין ילוה ובין לא ילוה מ"מ דילמא היה תנאי אתו שלא יתחייב רק שעבודו יחול תיכף ואם יהיה בידו יש לו מגו דקלתי' או פרעי' משא"כ אם אינו בידו ולכך המוצא יחזיר דל"ל מיגו:
urim_vetumim_tumim.en:
And one who acquires through kinyan, etc. Maggid Mishneh explains that where the borrower made a kinyan before the lender was present, the lender cannot simply tell witnesses afterward, "Write the document and keep it until the borrower agrees," because until the borrower gives proper authorization there is concern that the writing is only an appearance of falsehood. Shach challenges this. He argues that we do not generally fear a mere appearance of falsehood where the underlying transaction is true. He also points out that the Mishnah's rule, "we do not write a document for the lender when the borrower is absent," must be understood differently according to Abaye. According to Rav Asi, who establishes the first clause as involving acquisition documents, one can understand why the second clause teaches that the lender cannot have a document written without the borrower. But Abaye holds that omission of warranty is a scribal error and does not establish the first clause only as a kinyan case. If the Mishnah's second clause merely taught the obvious rule that the lender cannot create a document without the borrower's consent, what novelty remains? It is forced to say that even for Abaye the Mishnah shifts between different types of documents without saying so. The better explanation is as follows. Maggid Mishneh's rule depends upon a concern of apparent falsehood. Shach rejects that concern. If so, according to ordinary law, where the lender says to witnesses, "Prepare the document and keep it until the borrower later agrees," there would be no reason to prohibit the writing merely because the borrower has not yet given his final instruction. That works according to Rav Asi in a case with kinyan. But according to Abaye, who explains why one may write for the borrower while the lender is absent through the principle that the witnesses acquire for the lender through their signatures, the timing of the signatures is crucial. "His witnesses acquire for him through their signatures" means that at the moment the witnesses sign, they act under the borrower's authorization and thereby create the creditor's right. If the lender had them sign merely as a draft, before the borrower ever instructed them to sign, the signatures were not made as the borrower's agents and cannot operate to acquire anything for the lender. Later borrower consent cannot retroactively transform those old signatures into signatures made under his command. The result could therefore be an antedated document. The lien date would appear to be the earlier date of signing, even though the borrower did not authorize the creation of the creditor's right until later. Abaye's principle cannot cure that. Thus the Mishnah teaches: One may write a document for the borrower while the lender is absent because, when the borrower instructs the witnesses to sign, the signatures themselves acquire for the lender. But one may not write for the lender while the borrower is absent, even if the lender says, "Prepare it now and give it to me only after he agrees," because the old signatures were not made under the borrower's command and therefore do not acquire from their date. This creates a genuine antedating concern. Now the Mishnah is meaningful under both Abaye and Rav Asi. This also explains why the Gemara's difficulty is directed only according to Rav Asi in the kinyan framework. Rav Asi does not use Abaye's "witnesses acquire through their signatures" solution. Where a kinyan already occurred, the underlying lien may already exist and there is less reason to fear antedating merely because the paper was prepared earlier. If we also reject concern for appearance of falsehood, why should the lender not prepare a document and hold it pending the borrower's final consent? The answer must then be that a standard kinyan intended for writing is perhaps effective only where the lender himself was present at the kinyan, or under some equivalent condition. That is the Ramban-based limitation. But this means one should not combine both stringencies indiscriminately. Either the rule is based on appearance of falsehood as Maggid Mishneh says, or it is based on Ramban's narrower view of when a kinyan stands for writing. The sources do not establish both together as cumulative requirements. Indeed, Rashba and Raah disagree with Ramban on the latter point. Therefore there is no basis to impose both concerns except according to Sema's unusually strict reading. At least where a kinyan was made in the lender's absence and the lender later asks witnesses to prepare a document to be held until the borrower authorizes delivery, there is substantial ground to permit once the underlying lien already exists and no antedating results. There is no "appearance of falsehood" because the debt and lien are real. Moreover, the very rule is disputed, and we should not invent a double stringency unsupported by the major poskim. I remain somewhat uncertain for another reason. If a document is written and signed entirely without the borrower's authorization, why is it not invalid as "from their writing" altogether? As I explained above, written testimony ordinarily requires either authorization that gives it documentary status or another recognized legal mechanism. If the writing was originally worthless, how can the borrower's later statement "write" validate it retroactively? Why should an instruction given an hour later differ from one given months later? If later authorization could retroactively turn worthless writing into a document, one could revive any old paper that had never had legal force. This problem actually supports the view I stated above in seif 3. The debtor's instruction "write" is not necessarily what makes the testimony itself valid in the first place. Where the writing was prepared in normal legal document form, it can already preserve the underlying testimony. The debtor's authorization is needed primarily because creating a written loan against him strengthens the creditor's collection rights and should not be done against his will. On that understanding, later consent on the same day can indeed authorize the documentary consequence without needing to "revive" dead testimony. The witnesses' evidence was always valid in substance; what was missing was permission to impose written-loan status. This fits Maggid Mishneh far better. Ramban may disagree conceptually and require authorization already at the time of writing, but then his view should not be combined with Maggid Mishneh's separate appearance-of-falsehood reasoning as though both were universally accepted. Shach, who rejects Maggid Mishneh here, later in siman 48 leans toward Rashi's view that even the operative text of a document should not be written before the borrower commands it. His positions are therefore not entirely consistent. Accordingly, I do not accept Sema's cumulative stringency. The halachah should follow the more moderate structure explained above. There is another consequence of this analysis concerning the apparent contradiction between Maggid Mishneh and Ramban. Maggid Mishneh's concern is that writing before the borrower's authorization may look false because, at the moment of writing, the paper states a transaction that has not yet been formally authorized as a written loan. Ramban's concern is different. He addresses whether an ordinary kinyan itself stands for writing when the beneficiary was absent. These are separate questions. If the kinyan itself already created the lien and is sufficiently public, then the document can later be written without creating a false substantive statement. The underlying obligation exists. If, however, the kinyan does not stand for writing in that posture, the creditor may still need the borrower's later command before the paper becomes a creditor document. One should not infer from the existence of the second problem that the first must also be present. This matters because Sema treats both as if they reinforce one another and therefore creates an unusually strict rule. But if Rashba and Raah reject Ramban's limitation, and Shach rejects the concern of apparent falsehood, what remains as a source for the combined stringency? Nothing clear. The practical halachah should therefore distinguish the cases. If the borrower already made a valid kinyan that, according to the accepted local practice and authorities, stands for writing, there is strong basis to prepare the document even if the lender was not present at the kinyan, provided the paper is not delivered in a manner contrary to the borrower's remaining rights. If there was no such kinyan and the lender merely asks the witnesses to prepare a form in advance, Abaye's antedating concern remains substantial because the signatures were not made under the borrower's authority. There is also an important conceptual difference between the substantive debt and the document's lien date. Suppose the borrower owes the money orally already. The witnesses later prepare a document without his instruction. Their writing may truthfully record an existing debt. Nevertheless, if the document is dated from the earlier day and later delivered as a written loan, it can improperly create collection from purchasers from a time when no written lien existed. Thus a document can be factually true yet legally antedated. This is precisely why the issue cannot be reduced to "appearance of falsehood." The paper may contain no factual lie at all. The problem is that its legal consequences can reach backward beyond the moment of authorization. Abaye's rule solves that only where the signatures themselves, made under the borrower's authority, acquire for the lender from their date. If the signatures were placed earlier without authorization, they cannot later be given that retroactive effect. This further supports the explanation above. By contrast, where a kinyan already created a lien from the earlier date, later writing merely memorializes a preexisting legal state. There is then no antedating. The later paper does not create a new retroactive lien; it records one already born through the kinyan. This is why the kinyan case is fundamentally different. One can also understand the dispute about writing a document for a seller or giver in the same way. In a completed sale or gift by kinyan, the property already changed hands. A later document can record that completed transfer. The grantor may still have a right to prevent creation of a stronger evidentiary paper if the original arrangement did not authorize one, but there is no issue of creating the property transfer retroactively. That is why Rosh can say the grantor may retract from the writing but not from the field itself. In a loan, the document can affect not only proof but also the creditor's rights against purchasers. The stakes are therefore greater, and authorization matters more. This difference explains why statements concerning gifts and sales cannot always be transferred mechanically to loans. Nevertheless, where the loan kinyan itself already created the relevant lien, the analogy becomes much closer. There is another indication from the rule that omission of warranty is a scribal error. If the borrower authorized a written loan, the document can collect from encumbered property even if the warranty language was accidentally omitted. That rule shows the legal force of the document depends not merely upon the words physically written but upon the transaction the witnesses were authorized to memorialize. Authorization therefore links the paper to the legal event. Where the paper was signed before any authorization, that link is missing. Later consent can perhaps authorize delivery prospectively, but it should not automatically make the old signatures operate retroactively from their date unless the underlying kinyan already supplied the lien. This is another reason Abaye's mechanism cannot be extended too far. Accordingly, the cleanest framework is: Where no prior kinyan or lien exists, signatures placed without the borrower's instruction cannot later be used to create a retroactive written lien from the signing date. Where a prior kinyan already created the lien, later writing can generally record that existing status, subject to the dispute whether the kinyan stood for writing in the creditor's absence. Where the writing is merely a draft or memorandum and no one seeks retroactive lien consequences, the concern is much weaker and can depend upon the broader dispute concerning written testimony discussed above. This framework harmonizes Abaye, Rav Asi, Rosh, Ramban, Maggid Mishneh, and Shach more naturally than imposing every stringency simultaneously.
Or if he wrote explicitly in the document that the property will be encumbered from now, etc. Shach leaves this law unresolved. Ran derives it from Rashi in Ketubot 19b. Rashi explains a case where witnesses say, "It was a trust document." He describes a document that had been written before any loan occurred, with the borrower already subjecting his property from now for a loan that might be advanced later. Since the lien begins immediately, the document is not antedated when the loan is eventually made, although there can be another prohibition involved in leaving such a document outstanding. Ran derives that if the borrower expressly subjects his property from now for a future loan, witnesses may write even when the lender is not presently there, although the document is not a standard kinyan document. Shach asks that Rashi's case involved the document being delivered immediately to the lender. The lien can therefore begin from now. Where the lender is absent and the document remains with the witnesses, what source is there that the same rule applies? One cannot answer that Ran means merely that the lender had not yet advanced the money but the document itself was already delivered to him. Ran does not need to teach that. Ran himself does not follow Rashi's special requirement that the money be seen or advanced at the same moment. Like most authorities, he holds that once a proper document is delivered to the lender, we need not supervise when the money is actually handed over. Nimukei Yosef cites him to that effect, and if the borrower says explicitly, "Acquire for the lender," it certainly works. Thus Ran must be teaching a case where the document can be written even before delivery to the lender. Shach's difficulty therefore requires an answer. The key lies in Rosh's objection to Rif in the first chapter of Bava Metzia. Rif explains "documents of acquisition" simply as documents containing a kinyan. Rosh asks: why should kinyan make any difference? Once a document says, "So-and-so borrowed one hundred from so-and-so," the borrower's property is subject to the creditor under the ordinary rules even without a kinyan. If publicity is the issue, the witnesses to the document create publicity, not the kinyan itself. At first glance Rosh's question is very difficult. The entire concern of the Gemara is that perhaps the borrower asked to have the document written but never actually borrowed. If no money was advanced and the document never reached the lender, what obligation or lien exists at all? My relative, the famous gaon Maharam Schiff, already raised this and left Rosh's words requiring study. One cannot explain Rosh's question by saying the borrower expressly admitted, "I already owe this creditor one hundred," because then the case is not the ordinary fear that he wrote in order to borrow later. Nor can we say the witnesses knew the money had already been advanced, because that empties the Gemara's concern of content. Rosh also follows Rabbenu Tam below in siman 40 that merely saying, "I owe you one hundred in a document," does not create a new obligation until a document reaches the creditor. Thus a bare oral statement cannot solve the problem. The correct explanation is that even Rav Asi, who disagrees with Abaye regarding publicity, can agree with the underlying principle that witnesses can create the substantive acquisition and lien through their signatures. There are two separate questions: When does the legal obligation or lien arise? When does sufficient publicity arise to allow collection from purchasers? R. Meir holds that signed witnesses make the document operative. According to that theory, once the witnesses sign under proper authorization, the substantive legal creation can occur through the signatures themselves. This is the core of "his witnesses acquire for him through their signatures." Abaye holds the signatures also create sufficient publicity immediately. Rav Asi can disagree only on that second point. He may concede that the substantive lien exists through the signatures, while holding that the public does not treat the lien as announced until the creditor receives the document or until some additional unusual circumstance causes publicity. This explains Rosh. Rosh asks Rif: if the kinyan merely creates a property lien, that does not distinguish the case. The witnesses' signatures already create the substantive lien under R. Meir's document theory. The real distinction must therefore be publicity. Rav Asi says ordinary signatures, before the creditor receives the document and before money is advanced, do not generate sufficient public notice. A special acquisition document is different because the borrower undertakes liability in an unusual form, such as subjecting himself regardless of whether the future loan is ultimately advanced. Such an unusual transaction generates publicity from the outset. Rosh therefore explains Rashi's "shtarei aknayata" as a document in which the borrower subjects himself or his property whether he eventually borrows or not. Rosh calls this unusual, and precisely because it is unusual, word spreads. Now Rashi's view in Ketubot becomes clear. If the borrower expressly says, "My property is encumbered to you from now for whatever loan you later advance," the substantive lien is created now by the signatures. The unusual immediate encumbrance also generates publicity. There is therefore no antedating. It is irrelevant whether the lender physically holds the paper at that moment, because the legal lien and the publicity both already exist. This is the foundation of Ran's derivation. Shach's objection assumes that delivery to the lender is what creates the substantive effect. According to the Rosh-Rashi structure, that is not necessarily so. The signatures can create the substantive lien; delivery matters mainly for ordinary publicity under Rav Asi. Where the document expressly creates an immediate encumbrance from now, the unusual nature of the arrangement supplies the publicity even without delivery. There is support from Ketubot 94b. R. Meir says that where one document was written first and another delivered first, the one written first can acquire priority because witnesses to the signatures are the operative act. Maharsha asks: according to Rav Asi, who does not accept "his witnesses acquire through their signatures" in the ordinary loan context, why should earlier writing matter? The answer must be that under R. Meir, where signed witnesses are the operative legal act, everyone accepts the substantive acquisition through signatures. Rav Asi's dispute is only whether ordinary pre-delivery signatures have enough publicity in a loan to collect from purchasers. Maharsha himself, in Bava Metzia 20a, suggests that Tosafot's statement that "his witnesses acquire through their signatures" is a rabbinic enactment applies according to R. Elazar, who holds delivery witnesses create the instrument. According to R. Meir, signatures are the operative act by law itself. If so, we should not multiply the dispute by saying Rav Asi rejects even R. Meir's basic mechanism. This also explains why Rosh and Rashi can speak of immediate encumbrance without a kinyan act independent of the document. The document itself, through its signed operative form, can create the commitment. Rosh's phrase "whether he borrows or does not borrow" means that the borrower makes a present absolute undertaking whose existence does not depend upon later advancement of money. The actual collection can still be related to the eventual loan or condition, but the property lien arises immediately. Because that is unusual, it has publicity. One can now answer another major question posed against Rashi. Why should Rav Asi ever need actual advancement of money if the lender already received the signed document? Is delivery of the paper not at least as strong as Abaye's theory that signatures alone acquire for the creditor? According to the analysis above, Rav Asi's concern is not substantive acquisition but publicity. Abaye says the signed document itself creates public notice from the moment of signing. Rav Asi says that in an ordinary loan, until the lender actually advances the money, people do not treat the paper as evidence of a real outstanding debt. Even if the lender physically possesses it, the public can think it was prepared for a contemplated loan that never occurred. Therefore he requires the loan to become real before ordinary publicity arises. But if the document itself creates an extraordinary immediate lien from now regardless of whether the loan is advanced at once, the unusual transaction is public enough from the outset. This is why Rashi's immediate-encumbrance clause matters even after delivery. Mishneh LaMelech asks why Rashi needs to say the property is encumbered from now if the lender already holds the document. He assumes delivery alone should solve the antedating concern. He overlooked that Rashi consistently requires the advance of money as well. Rashi's explanations elsewhere show this. At the beginning of Rosh Hashanah concerning dating documents by regnal years, Rashi explains a case where the loan was seen in Tammuz and the document was signed in Kislev, creating uncertainty whether the paper is antedated. If delivery of the document on the day it was written automatically cured the issue regardless of when the money was advanced, Rashi's example would not work in that way. The fact that it does shows Rashi requires the underlying loan to become real, not merely physical possession of the paper. Thus Ran's derivation is much stronger than Shach assumed. If the borrower creates an immediate encumbrance from now, the same reason that helps when the document is in the lender's hand also helps when it remains with the witnesses: the substantive lien and the publicity already exist. Still, although we have defended Ran within Rashi and Rosh, Rama should not have stated the law as unquestionably settled. The entire analysis depends on a major premise: even Rav Asi agrees that under R. Meir the signatures can create the substantive lien before delivery, and his disagreement with Abaye is only about publicity. Not all authorities accept that. Ramban, as cited by Baal HaTerumot and in his discussion at the end of Perek HaMegareish, holds more broadly that according to Rav Asi we do not say "his witnesses acquire through their signatures" even under R. Meir. He uses this to reconcile Rif, who rules that signed witnesses are operative, with Shmuel's rule that where two documents have the same date the court uses judicial discretion. If earlier writing automatically created the right, discretion would be unnecessary. Ramban answers that because we rule like Rav Asi, the right does not arise until the document reaches the recipient. This is explicit. According to Ramban, Ran's derivation from Rashi cannot be treated as universal. It depends on how one understands Rav Asi and the document theory. Thus Shach is correct in the bottom line that Rama's ruling is subject to dispute, although the reason is not that Ran misunderstood Rashi. Ran's law is coherent and well grounded within the Rashi-Rosh approach. The practical result is a genuine safek among the Rishonim. There is a further refinement. The entire theory that even Rav Asi accepts substantive acquisition through signatures is strongest under R. Meir, who holds signed witnesses make the instrument. According to R. Elazar, who holds delivery witnesses are operative, Abaye's "his witnesses acquire through their signatures" is itself a rabbinic enactment. Tosafot say so. If Rav Asi rejects that enactment, then under R. Elazar there is no reason to say the signatures themselves create substantive acquisition before delivery. Many poskim rule like R. Elazar in document law. Accordingly, even if Ran's rule is sound under R. Meir, its general application under our halachic framework becomes more doubtful. This also explains why Rav Asi's establishment of "documents of acquisition" may be forced into a special form where the borrower makes an absolute present commitment independent of ordinary document delivery. Under R. Elazar's system, a regular signed paper still needs delivery. Only an independent kinyan or another substantive present undertaking can create the lien earlier. This is another reason to treat Rama's ruling as doubtful rather than absolute. There is also a practical distinction between a document saying, "My property is encumbered from now when you later lend," and one saying, "I absolutely obligate myself from now whether you lend or not." The latter is a full present obligation and, according to Rashi's "shtarei aknayata" explanation, can clearly generate the unusual publicity Rosh describes. The former is only a present lien conditional on a future loan. Ran reads Rashi as permitting this as well. But according to authorities who require a complete present acquisition to produce publicity, the conditional form may be weaker. This helps explain why Rashi and Rosh often describe shtarei aknayata in the extreme form, "whether he lends or does not lend." They are not merely saying the property will be collateral for a future loan. They are saying the borrower creates a present absolute obligation so unusual that everyone recognizes its immediate legal effect. One cannot infer every conditional future encumbrance from that language without dispute. This distinction is important in applying Rama's ruling. Accordingly, the law should be treated as follows: Where the borrower makes a complete present kinyan or absolute present obligation, the witnesses may write because the lien and publicity begin immediately. Where he merely writes that property will be encumbered from now for a loan to be advanced later, Ran and Rashi support validity, but Ramban and other authorities create substantial doubt. One should therefore not extract from purchasers in a doubtful case contrary to the possessor's claim. The matter is a true safek among the poskim.
And they wrote for him. Bach, Sema, and Shach infer from this wording that Tur too requires the kinyan to have been made in the creditor's presence; otherwise an ordinary kinyan does not stand for writing. This is difficult according to Tur's own adoption of Rosh's interpretation of "shtarei aknayata." As explained above, Rosh does not define the phrase as an ordinary kinyan document. He explains it as a document creating an absolute present obligation, whether the future loan is actually advanced or not. If so, Ramban's proof from the Mishnah does not apply directly to Tur. Ramban reasons from the clause, "we do not write a document for the creditor unless the borrower is with him." He says this must be teaching that even where a kinyan occurred, if it was not in the creditor's presence it does not automatically authorize writing. But according to Rosh and Tur, the Mishnah's first clause is not speaking of an ordinary kinyan at all. It is speaking of the unusual absolute-acquisition document just described. Then of course the later clause still requires the borrower to say "write." Nothing can be inferred about an ordinary kinyan conducted outside the creditor's presence. One might try to derive Ramban's rule from the sale and gift clauses instead. There, Rosh agrees that a completed kinyan transfers the field immediately and the grantor cannot retract the property even if the document remains with him. Rosh says so expressly in responsum klal 66, and Tur likewise rules below in siman 250 concerning a gift made by kinyan. Yet it is forced to say the Mishnah uses "write for the borrower" and "write for the seller" in entirely different legal senses without indication. There is another proof that Rosh likely does not accept Ramban's requirement. In Perek HaSefinah, concerning "Acquire the field for so-and-so and write him a document," Rosh asks why the grantor can retract from the document if an ordinary kinyan stands for writing. The language "for so-and-so" implies the beneficiary is not present. Had Rosh accepted Ramban's rule that a kinyan outside the beneficiary's presence does not stand for writing, there would be no question. Likewise, in Perek Chezkas HaBatim, Rosh asks why after the party says "write and sign and give," and a kinyan is made, renewed consultation is needed, since an ordinary kinyan stands for writing. Again, the case can involve a beneficiary who is absent. Rosh does not distinguish. This strongly suggests Rosh rejects Ramban's limitation. Beit Yosef and Ir Shushan understand Tur this way, despite Tur later citing Ramban's view in siman 238. Tur may cite Ramban there as an additional opinion without adopting it as his father's own view. Accordingly, one should not infer from Tur's phrase "and they wrote for him" that he requires the creditor's presence at the kinyan. The matter remains disputed, and Rosh's language leans against Ramban.
And the creditor shall not acquire until the borrower instructs that it be given. This ruling requires study. Rama copied it from Tur. If the borrower says, "Make a kinyan and give the document into my hand," and the creditor acquires nothing until the borrower later orders delivery, then the Mishnah's rule, "we write a document for the borrower even when the creditor is not with him," can be explained simply: the borrower says, "Make the kinyan and give me the paper." Rosh says exactly this in responsum klal 66 when explaining Rambam's law of a borrower who deposited his document with a third party and died. Rosh says that in a loan, because the Mishnah permits writing for the borrower without the creditor, we must fear that perhaps no actual loan ever occurred. Rambam's case therefore involves a kinyan, because without a kinyan one would not write for the borrower alone. If so, the old difficulty against Rif returns in full. Rif holds that even in a kinyan document the creditor must ultimately receive the document. His later critics ask from the rule that if one finds a kinyan document in the street, it is returned to the creditor because the borrower already subjected himself. If physical delivery is still required, perhaps the document fell from the borrower and the creditor never acquired anything. The generation after Rif therefore explained the law differently, saying that the found document case proves a kinyan document does not require prior delivery. If Rama's rule is correct, their objection to Rif disappears. A borrower often has a kinyan document prepared and kept in his own hands before any loan occurs. If such a document is found, why should it ever be returned to the creditor without first asking the borrower? The concern is not rare. The Mishnah itself says this is the ordinary procedure: a document may be written for the borrower while the creditor is absent. The Gemara repeatedly worries about precisely that possibility in cases of found documents and parties with identical names. Therefore Rama's rule is hard to reconcile with the accepted interpretation of the found-kiniyan-document sugya. In truth, Tur and Rosh themselves do not prove Rama's broad rule. Their interpretation of "shtarei aknayata" differs from Rif's. They explain the phrase as an absolute obligation created whether the future loan is advanced or not. In that special document, there is no difficulty returning a found paper to the creditor, because the borrower is already obligated regardless of delivery. At the same time, Tur can still say that an ordinary kinyan made for a contemplated loan does not give the creditor rights in the physical document until delivery. Thus there is no contradiction within Rosh and Tur's own system. But we do not generally follow their narrow definition of shtarei aknayata. Most authorities understand it as an ordinary document containing a kinyan. On that understanding, the found-document sugya proves that the creditor's substantive right can exist even before physical delivery. Baal HaTerumot, Shaar 52, says expressly that this question depends upon the dispute between Rif and the later authorities. Nimukei Yosef likewise explains Rashi's language in terms of an ordinary kinyan and says such a kinyan already creates the creditor's right. Or Zarua is even more explicit. Therefore Rama's unqualified statement should not have been copied as settled law. Beit Yosef did well to omit it. One might rescue Rama by reading his words more narrowly. Perhaps "the creditor does not acquire" means only that he does not acquire the physical document itself. The underlying debt and property lien have already become binding through the kinyan. This would be analogous to the rule that after a gift is acquired, the grantor can still retract from having a separate deed written while unable to retract the transferred field. Then the found kinyan document can still be returned, because the creditor already owns the underlying claim and the paper merely evidences it. The borrower can say, "Give the document to me," without retaining a migo that no debt exists. This interpretation would solve much. But Beit Yosef in Bedek HaBayit reads Tur and Rama more broadly. He writes that where the borrower says, "Give it into my hand," the witnesses may not give it to the creditor because the borrower did not complete his intent to subject himself until the loan would actually be advanced. If they deliver it earlier, they wrong him. That clearly treats the substantive obligation as incomplete, not merely ownership of the paper. Tur's language also tends toward that reading. Accordingly, the narrow rescue is difficult. There is another possibility. Even if the borrower becomes obligated through the kinyan from the beginning, while the paper remains in his hand he has a migo to destroy it or to say the condition for the obligation was never fulfilled. Once the document leaves his possession, that migo disappears. Then the creditor's position becomes practically enforceable without saying the legal obligation arose only at delivery. This can reconcile some formulations. Suppose the borrower conditioned that the loan would be advanced later but made the property lien effective immediately. If he still holds the document, he can claim the condition failed and destroy the evidence. If the paper is found outside his possession, however, his ability to make that claim is impaired. The found-document rule can therefore allow return even though delivery has evidentiary importance. Still, this is not the plain sense of Rama. The main conclusion remains that the matter is disputed. Under the majority interpretation of shtarei aknayata, a proper kinyan creates the substantive right even before delivery to the creditor. Rama's broader statement, that the creditor acquires nothing until the borrower orders delivery, is doubtful. One should therefore follow Beit Yosef's caution and not treat the ruling as universally settled. See further below in siman 55.

urim_vetumim_urim.he:
כותבים שטר וכו' כשכותבין בלשון דמשמע דהיה הלוה לבדו א"צ להכיר המלוה רק הלוה סמ"ע:
אין כותבין בע"כ דלא ניחא לי' דליפוק עליה קלא של עושר ולהשביע אותו ופשוט:
כתבו השטר וחתמוהו כו' דהטעם משום מחזי כשקרא ובכתיבה ליכא כדלקמן סימן מ"ח ועיין תומים מ"ש בקושי' הש"ך וכתב הסמ"ע אפילו באמת כבר קנו מן הלוה רק היה שלא בפני המלוה הואיל דקנין שלא בפני המלוה לאו לכתיבה עומד כדלעיל סעיף ד' אם יאמר המלוה כתבו ויהיה בידכם עד שיצוה הלוה ליתנו מ"מ לא יעשו כך. ואני כתבתי בתומים דבכה"ג ליכא למיחש ובפרט דליכא מחזי כשקרא כיון דגוף הדבר אמת דכבר נעשה קנין ע"כ וע"ש שכתבתי דכמעט דעת הרמב"ן והמ"מ סותרים אהדדי ע"ש:
להקנות ממנו פי' היום דאל"כ הא ה"ל מוקדם דלא חל שעבודו רק משעת קנין סמ"ע וצ"ל להקנות ממנו מיותר דהל"ל סתמא אם יסכים תנהו לי' ושיגרא דלישנא נקיט:
בשטר שיש בו קנין כו' הסמ"ע והש"ך כולם תמהו שלא הזכיר המחבר ורמ"א דעת התו' ורא"ש דא"צ לקנין רק קי"ל כאביי עבחז"ל והעלו דיכול המוחזק לומר קים ליה כמ"ד עבחז"ל והנכון אתם אך בגוף עבחז"ל אי אמרינן אף במכר ושובר כן ואי בעינן בכל דוכתי מטו לידו עיין מ"ש לקמן בסי' ס"ה כי שם הארכתי בתומים ובררתי הדברים בס"ד:
או שכתוב בשטר וכו' עיין תומים מ"ש בזה ליישב תמיהת הש"ך על הר"ן ומ"מ העליתי לדינא כי הך דינא ספיקא דדינא ותלוי במחלוקת רבוותא ע"ש:
עד שיהיה מלוה עמו ה"ה אם אמר לעדים שיזכו בשטר בשביל המלוה ויהיה בידם בשביל המלוה ליתן לו כשירצה המלוה הרי הן שלוחי מלוה והוי כאילו מלוה עמו נ"י והביאו סמ"ע והש"ך:
ויתן השטר ביד המלוה כו' לאפוקי מדעת התוס' גיטין דף י"ז ע"ב ד"ה עד שעת וכו' דכתבו אם המלוה עם הלוה אין להעדים צורך להשגיח אם נמסר למלוה דמסתמא ימסרו לו אבל דעת שארי מחברים דצריכין דוקא למסור לידו סמ"ע:
ביד המלוה כו' אפילו לא ראו נתינת המעות כל שנמסר ליד מלוה אין לחוש יותר ודלא כדעת רש"י דבעי גם כן ראיה דנמסר לו המעות:
או ילוה וכו' פי' כשראו נתינת המעות דלא שייך שמא לא ילוה מכל מקום שייך שמא לא ימסור לו השטר ואם כן לא טריף רק מזמן מסירה ולא מקודם כהנ"ל ומכ"ש שלא ראו מסירת המעות דיש לחוש תרתי שמא לא ילוה וגם לא ימסור אבל באמת הכל תלוי במסירה כמ"ש דאם נמסר אף דלא לוהו עדיין לית לן ביה:
וכתבו לו מזו דייקו הסמ"ע וב"ח דאף דהיה הקנין מכל מקום הואיל ושלא בפני מלוה נעשית לאו לכתיבה עומד כדעת הרמב"ן ומחבר לעיל סוף סעיף ד' ולכך בעי לומר כתבו ועיין תומים מ"ש בזה בדעת הרא"ש:
ולא יזכה וכו' עיין תומים שהעליתי דין זה בצ"ע כי נראה ברור אם יש בו קנין מכל מקום אף דנתנו לידו מכל מקום חייב לשלם רק חוזר בשטר דהא כיון דעשה קנין הרי סתמא מתחייב בין ילוה בין לא ילוה כלל וא"כ מה מהני דנמסר ליד לוה ע"ש:
עד שיצא מתחת כו' ואז זכה בו המלוה משעת הקנין לכ"ע ש"ך:
urim_vetumim_urim.en:
They write a document, etc. When the wording makes clear that the borrower alone appeared, the witnesses need identify only the borrower, not the lender. Sema.
They do not write it against his will. A lender may object because he does not want a reputation of wealth to spread about him and thereby expose him to demands. This is obvious.
They wrote and signed the document, etc. The concern is that it appears false. Mere writing does not create that appearance, as explained below in siman 48. See Tumim concerning the Shach's difficulty. Sema writes that even if a kinyan was actually made from the borrower, but it occurred in the lender's absence, since a kinyan made outside the lender's presence does not automatically stand for writing, as explained above in seif 4, the witnesses should not comply even if the lender says, "Write it and keep it with you until the borrower instructs you to deliver it." In Tumim I wrote that in such a case there is no reason for concern, especially because there is no appearance of falsehood since the underlying transaction is true and the kinyan already occurred. See there, where I noted that the positions of Ramban and Maggid Mishneh almost contradict each other.
To make a kinyan from him. Meaning, to make the kinyan today. Otherwise the document would be antedated, since the lien begins only at the time of the kinyan. Sema. The words "to make a kinyan from him" are really unnecessary, since the text could simply have said, "If he agrees, give it to him." It is merely conventional phrasing.
In a document containing a kinyan, etc. Sema and Shach both question why the Mechaber and Rama did not mention the view of Tosafos and Rosh that no kinyan is required because we rule like Abaye that a witness's signature effects acquisition. They conclude that the party in possession may say that he relies upon the opinion that a witness's signature effects acquisition, and they are correct. As to the underlying rule, whether it applies also to a sale document and a receipt, and whether in every context the document must actually reach the recipient's hand, see what I wrote below in siman 65, where I discussed these matters at length in Tumim and clarified them with God's help.
Or if it is written in the document, etc. See Tumim, where I resolved the Shach's difficulty with the Ran. Nevertheless, I concluded for practical halachah that this rule remains a legal doubt dependent upon a dispute among the authorities. See there.
Until the lender is with him. The same applies if the lender instructs the witnesses to acquire the document on his behalf and to hold it for him until he wishes to receive it. They then serve as the lender's agents and it is as though the lender were present. Nimukei Yosef, cited by Sema and Shach.
And he gives the document into the lender's hand, etc. This excludes Tosafos in Gittin 17b, s.v. "until the time," who write that if lender and borrower are together, the witnesses need not supervise actual delivery because it may be presumed that the document will be handed over. Other authorities require actual delivery into the lender's hand. Sema.
Into the lender's hand, etc. Even if the witnesses did not see the money being given, once the document was delivered to the lender there is no further concern. This is unlike Rashi, who also requires the witnesses to see the money delivered.
Or he will lend, etc. Meaning that even where they saw the money being given, so there is no concern that the loan might not occur, there remains a concern that the borrower may not deliver the document. In that case the creditor may seize purchasers only from the date of delivery, not from the earlier date. All the more so where the witnesses did not see the money, for there are two concerns, that the loan may never occur and that the document may never be delivered. In truth, however, everything depends upon delivery. If the document was delivered, it makes no difference that the money had not yet been lent, as explained above.
And they shall write for him. From this Sema and Bach infer that even where a kinyan occurred, if it was made outside the lender's presence it does not automatically stand for writing, in accordance with Ramban and the Mechaber above at the end of seif 4. Therefore the borrower must expressly say, "Write." See Tumim concerning the Rosh's view.
And he shall not acquire, etc. See Tumim, where I left this law requiring study. It appears clear that if there was a kinyan, then even if the document was subsequently returned to the borrower, he nevertheless remains liable to pay, and only the document itself reverts to him. Once he made a kinyan, he ordinarily undertook liability whether or not the loan ultimately occurred. What then is achieved by delivering the document back to the borrower? See there.
Until it leaves the possession of, etc. At that point the lender acquires the rights retroactively from the time of the kinyan according to all opinions. Shach.

mechaber.he: חייב עצמו לשנים בקנין ואמר לעדים שיכתבו ויתנו בידו וכן עשו ומסר החייב השטר לא' מהם אע"פ שלא ידע האחר מזו המסירה ואפילו מת ולא ידע זכה בחלקו ויגבוהו היתומים:
mechaber.en: He had to say to the years in Klanin and told witnesses that he would write and give him his hand, and he had made a message that he had no knowledge of the other than that of the petitioner and even dead, and he did not know that he was partially and the highest of the orphans:

baer_hetev.he: זכה. כתב הש"ך דצ"ע דהמעיין היטב בבעה"ת שם יראה דמיירי במחייב עצמו לשנים בסתם ולא אמר לעדים כלום ומסרו העדים השטר לאחד מהם וגם בזה נסתפק שם אבל אם החייב בעצמו מסרו לאחד מהם משמע דלא זכה בו אלא זה שנמסר לידו אבל האחר מנין יזכה ואולי גם הטור מיירי דמסרו לזה באופן שיזכה ג"כ לחבירו בחלקו וצ"ע עכ"ל:
baer_hetev.en: He acquired. The Shach writes that this requires study. One who carefully examines the Baal HaTerumot will see that he discusses a person who obligated himself generally to two people, said nothing to the witnesses, and the witnesses delivered the document to one of them. Even in that case the Baal HaTerumot remained uncertain. But if the obligor himself delivered it to one of them, it appears that only the recipient acquired rights through it. By what basis would the other acquire? Perhaps the Tur likewise means that he delivered it to one of them in a manner intended to confer the other person's share as well. This requires study.

beer_hagolah.he: ה) טור וכ"כ בעה"ת בשער נ"ב ששאל את ה' ר' נתן בר מאיר והשיב לו כזה
beer_hagolah.en: e) Tur, and so writes Baal HaTerumot, gate 52, that he asked Rabbi Natan bar Meir and received this ruling from him.

beur_hagra.he:
חייב. דזכין לאדם כו':
(ליקוט) חייב עצמו כו'. מתני' בב"ב שם זיכה לו ע"י אחר כו' ובקנין מיירי כנ"ל ומיירי ג"כ שלא ידע הזוכה דקתני רישא ונמצא כו' (ע"כ):
(ליקוט) ואפי' מת כו'. גטין ספ"א י"ד ב' תני חדא כו' לימא בהא כו' לימא הולך כזכי תנאי כו' וי"א הולך כזכי דמי כו' ע"ש כל הסוגי' ש"מ דבזכי לכ"ע יתן ליורשיו (ע"כ):
beur_hagra.en:
He obligated. Because one may acquire on behalf of a person even without his knowledge.
(Collected note) He obligated himself, etc. Mishnah in Bava Batra there: "he transferred it to him through another, etc." It concerns a kinyan, as above, and also where the beneficiary did not know, because the opening clause says "and it was found, etc." (End of collected note.)
(Collected note) And even if he died, etc. Gittin at the end of chapter 1, 14b: "one baraita teaches, etc.; let us say the dispute is, etc.; shall we say that 'take' is like 'acquire' according to Tannaim, etc.; some say 'take' is like 'acquire,' etc." See the entire sugya. We learn that where there is an actual acquisition on his behalf, all agree that it is given to his heirs. (End of collected note.)

netivot_hamishpat_beurim.he: ומסר החייב השטר והש"ך הניח זה בצ"ע ונראה דאפי' להמחבר דוקא בקנין דמשעת קנין זכו בו רק משום שאמר תנו בידי אמרינן דלא כוון בהקנין רק על תנאי דהיינו שיהיה למפרע ואחר שהתקיים התנאי אותו הדבר שבמחשבתו מש"ה אמרינן שלשון בידי שאמר דכונתו לא היה רק שכל זמן שיהיה השטר בידי לא יתחיל הקנין אבל כשמוציאו מתחת ידו להמתחייב אף שמסרו לא"מ ע"כ כבר נתקיים תנאו שהיה במחשבתו ובודאי לא היה כונתו בלשון תנו בידי רק לתנאי זה אבל בשטרי דלאו הקנאה רק שקונה אותו בשטר כשמטא לידיה ודאי דבעינן שיגיע ליד שניהם דשניה' צריכין לעשות קנין כמו במקדש או במגרש ב' נשים בשטר אחד או בשטר מתנה לב' אנשים ביחד דבעינן שיתן לזה ואח"כ לזה שיעשו שניהם הקנין ובקנין סתם ולא אמר תנו בידי לפי מה דקימ"ל דבשטר הקנאה בסתם לא בעינן מטא לידיה אין צורך להאי דינא כלל:
netivot_hamishpat_beurim.en: And the obligor delivered the document. Shach leaves this rule requiring study. According to Mechaber, where a kinyan already gave the recipient a retroactive right but the obligor said, 'Give the document to me,' his language is best understood as conditioning final effect on the instrument leaving his hands. Once he himself removes it from his possession and transfers it to the beneficiary, even through an intermediary, the condition has been fulfilled. But in a non-kinyan document where acquisition occurs only through receipt of the document itself, every beneficiary who must acquire through the deed must actually receive it. Thus a single document intended to transfer to two recipients must reach each according to ordinary acquisition law.

netivot_hamishpat_hidushim.he: זכה בחלקו דוקא בשטר קנין אפי' אמר תנו בידי דאז מהני מסירה לאחר אפי' אין שותפין בחוב אבל) (בשטר בלא קנין צריך שיהיה מטא ליד כל אחד אפי' למאן דס"ל עדים בחז"ל ואפי' בקנין הניח הש"ך דין זה בצ"ע:
netivot_hamishpat_hidushim.en: He was given in part at the Kennee Epi, he said, "Let my son take off after Aja, they do not have accomplices in the debt, but" (later without Kensen, there should be a sweep next to each of the epi's to Man, witnessing the IDF and Qinin put this sentence in the IDF:

rabbi_akiva_eiger.he: [ש"ך אות מא] דזכין לאדם שלא בפניו. נ"ב לכאורה נראה דתלי' בב' דעות לקמן סי' רמ"ג ס' י"א דלדעה א' שם דיכול לחזור היינו מטעם דא"א מקנה דבשלב"ל כמבואר בטור שם א"כ לא מהני הכאה שאומר לעדים שיזכו להמלוה להוציאו מדין מוקדם דהא אין העדים יכולין לזכות להמלוה דהא בשעת שאומר כן הלוה להעדים הוי דבשלב"ל וצ"ע:
rabbi_akiva_eiger.en: [Shach, letter 41] For one may acquire a benefit for a person in his absence. Note: At first glance this appears to depend upon the two opinions below, siman 243:11. According to the first opinion there, that he may retract because a person cannot transfer something that has not yet come into existence, as explained in the Tur there, it would not help here for the borrower to tell the witnesses to acquire on behalf of the creditor so as to remove the problem of an antedated document. The witnesses cannot acquire for the creditor, because at the time the borrower tells them to do so the relevant right has not yet come into existence. This requires study.

siftei_kohen.he:
חייב עצמו כו'. כן היא בטור ובב"י כתב שכיוצא בזה כתב הבעה"ת שער נ"ב ובאמת צ"ע דהמעיין היטב בבעה"ת שם סוף שער נ"ב יראה דמיירי במחייב עצמו לשנים בסתם ולא אמר לעדי' כלום ומסרו העדים השטר לאחד מהם וגם בזה פליג ה"ר יצחק שם והבע"ת נסתפק שם וה"ר נתן בן מאיר חולק שם על ה"ר יצחק בזה אבל היכא שאמר לעדים שוכתבו ויתנו השטר בידו וכן עשו ומסר החייב בעצמו לאחד מהם לא פליג ה"ר נתן בר"מ ואדרבא משמע שם דמודה ליה שהרי כתב ה"ר נתן שם דכשאמר להם קנו ממני וכתבו ותנו השטר לידי לא יזכה המלוה לעולם עד דמטא לידא דמקבל כו' עיין שם וא"כ נהי שמסרו החייב ניד האח' מכל מקום כיון שלא זכה בו המקבל מיד אין לך אלא מה שעשה החייב וזה שמסרו לו זכה בו אבל האחר שלא מסרו לו מנין יזכה ואולי גם הטור מיירי דכשמסרו לזה מסרו באופן שיזכה גם כן לחבירו בחלקו והיינו זיכה לו על ידי אחר שהזכיר ה"ר נתן שם ולא אתי אלא לאשמעינן דאפי' לא ידע האחר ממסירה זו ואפי' מת זכו היתומים בחלקו וצ"ע:
זכה בחלקו כו'. כתב הב"ח וז"ל. ונראה דטעמא דהאי דינא דכיון דנתחייב לשניהם בשטר ח' כשותפים נינהו וכל א' יכול לגבות כל החוב כולו וכדלקמן סי' ע"ז ס"י בהגה עכ"ד ולפע"ד ל"ד להתם דהתם מתחלה נעשו שותפים ביחד וזכו שניהם ביחד ונכתבו בשטר כן אבל הכא מאן לימא לן שזכה בו זה שלא מסרו לו כלל וכמ"ש בסמוך וגם בבעה"ת לא הוזכר טעם זה כלל אלא מיירי התם שלא אמר החייב תנו אותו בידי דנמצ' שזכה בו מיד משעת הקנין ע"ש ודו"ק:
siftei_kohen.en:
He obligated himself, etc. This is the Tur's text. The Beit Yosef says that the Baal HaTerumot writes a similar ruling in gate 52. Careful study shows otherwise. The Baal HaTerumot discusses one who obligated himself generally to two people, gave no instruction to the witnesses, and the witnesses delivered the document to one of them. Rabbi Yitzchak disputes that case, the Baal HaTerumot remains uncertain, and Rabbi Natan ben Meir disagrees with Rabbi Yitzchak. But where the obligor told the witnesses to write and place the document in his own hand, they did so, and he himself then delivered it to one recipient, Rabbi Natan does not dispute the result. Indeed, Rabbi Natan writes that when the obligor says, "Make a kinyan from me, write, and give the document into my hand," the creditor does not acquire until it reaches the recipient. Thus, even if the obligor delivered it to one creditor, the other did not acquire immediately. We have only what the obligor actually did: the person to whom he delivered it acquired, but what basis is there for the other to acquire? Perhaps the Tur speaks of a case in which delivery to the first was expressly made so that he should also acquire his colleague's share. This would be acquisition through another person, which Rabbi Natan mentions. The Tur would then teach that even if the second creditor never knew of the delivery, and even if he died, his heirs acquired his share. The matter requires study.
He acquired his share, etc. The Bach explains that because the obligor became liable to both creditors in one document, they are partners and each may collect the entire debt, as stated below in siman 77. In my opinion the cases are not comparable. There both became partners and acquired together from the outset, and the document was written accordingly. Here, who says that the creditor to whom the document was never delivered acquired anything? As I explained above, the Baal HaTerumot does not give the Bach's reason. His case is one in which the obligor did not say that the document should first be placed in his own hand, so both creditors acquired immediately through the kinyan. See there carefully.

turei_zahav.he: (ע"ש בב"י ד"ה לא לקח בקנין וכו' עד איכא מ"ד הלכתא כמר בר רב אשי וכו') ומ"ש התוספת בסנהדרין בשם ריב"ן שכתב בשם רש"י שפסק כמר בר"א באודיתא הוא ט"ס שרש"י בחולין פרק בהמה המקשה כתב להדיא דלית הלכתא באודיתא וכ"כ התוספת שם בשם רש"י וכ"כ הרא"ש שם בסנהדרין וכ"כ הנ"י בחולין בשם רש"י וע' שם וראיה ברורות מהוכחת הרא"ש מפ' הכותב דרש"י ס"ל דלית הילכתא כמר בר"א כו' ע"ש:
turei_zahav.en: (See the Beit Yosef, beginning “If he did not acquire through a kinyan, etc.” through “some rule like Mar bar Rav Ashi, etc.”) Tosafot in Sanhedrin cite Rivan in Rashi’s name as ruling like Mar bar Rav Ashi regarding an admission, but this is a scribal error. Rashi in Hullin explicitly rules that the halachah does not follow Mar bar Rav Ashi regarding an admission, and Tosafot there cite Rashi that way. The Rosh in Sanhedrin and the Nimukei Yosef in Hullin likewise report Rashi’s view. The Rosh’s proof from the chapter HaKotev establishes this clearly.

urim_vetumim_tumim.he: זכה בחלקו כו' הרב הש"ך השיג על דין זה דבלא"ה הך דינא במחלוקת שנוי' בבעה"ת שער נ"ב ואפילו הר' נתן ב"ם דס"ל הך דינא שם היינו בלא אומר לעדים שימסרו דוקא לידו אבל בהתנה שיתנו דוקא לידו נראה שם דמודה הר"נ ב"ם ג"כ דלא מהני רק לזה שנתן זוכה ולא השני אם לא שאמר לו שגם בעד חבירו יזכה דהיינו זיכה לו ע"י אחר שפי' הר"נ ב"ם הנ"ל עכ"ל. והנה באמת על המחבר אין לו תלונה כלל דכל דינו של הר"נ ב"ם הוא הכל על דרך ושיטת הרי"ף בקנין בעינן מטו לידו וכמ"ש שם להדיא ולכך אם אמר תנו בידי במה יזכה השני הא לא מטי לידו וכמ"ש שם באריכות. אבל לפי דקיי"ל כשיטת האחרונים החולקים על הרי"ף וסבירא להו דלא בעינן מטי לידו כלל אפילו בקנין הלואה וכמש"ל דכן מוכח מגמ' א"כ פשיטא דלא בעינן מטי לידו כלל והא דכתב דנתן לאחד מהם ולא קאמר אפילו תחת ידו ממש דהא לא בעינן מטי לידו היינו דהוא המתחייב חי ואם כן כ"ז ששטר בידו יש לו מגו דאי בעי' קלתי' לומר לא נתחייבתי לו כלל וכ"כ הרא"ש בתשובה כלל ס"ו הנ"ל אבל כשהוא ביד אחר לא שייך מגו ולק"מ למחבר אבל על הטור דסבירא ליה כמ"ש מקודם דבקנין בהלואה בעי מטו לידו וכמש"ל אם כן יש מקום לקושי' הש"ך כי מטו ליד אחר מה מהני לגבי שני. ובלא"ה אין כאן קושי' על הש"ע אפילו נימא דבעי בקנין מטו לידי' מכל מקום לא גרע ממתנת ש"מ ודייתקי דבעי' זכי' ואם קשור על יריכו לא יתן וכמ"ש הר"נ ב"מ ראי' מזו והמחבר פסק לקמן סי' ר"נ סעיף כ"ה דבנתן לבני אדם הרבה מתנה דאם זיכה לאחד דנתקיים מתנתו נגד כל היורשים דגילה דעתו שרוצה בקיום מתנה ע"ש סמ"ע ס"ק ע"א והר' נתן ב"מ יליף זה מזיכה לו ע"י אחר ואם כן כמו שהדין שם כך הדין כאן ודברי מחבר ברורים מכל צד ולא ה"ל הש"ך להעמיד דבריו על רבינו מחבר אמנם הטור דהשמיט לקמן בסי' ר"נ פירש הר"נ ב"ם על הך דזיכה לו ע"י אחר וכתב שם פי' רשב"ם וראב"ד ולא שת לבו לפי' הרמב"ם כמ"ש הסמ"ע קשה ולכן נראה ברור דמ"ש חייב עצמו לשנים בקנין היינו בחיוב גמור בין ילוה ובין לא ילוה וכן מורה לשון חייב עצמו היינו בהחלט בתורת מתנה ולא בתורת הלואה וכן מורה לשון זכה בו היינו במתנה גמורה דנתחייב להם בהחלט בין ילוה ובין לא ילוה וכן הוא בבע"ת שטר נ"ב שממנו מקורו דהכל במתנה ואם כן בהך שטר אקנייתא מבואר דלא יכול לחזור בו אפילו לא מטי לידי' כהנ"ל ואם כן פשיטא דזכה בו רק כ"ז שהוא תחת ידו אי' לי' מגו משא"כ ביוצא מתחת ידו לית ליה מגו כלל וזה שדייק הטור וכיון שיצא השטר מתחת יד החייב זכו בו שניהם ולא כתב כיון שזכה האחד זוכה ג"כ השני דהא לדעת הב"ח והש"ך הטעם דאחד זוכה בשביל חבירו ולמה כתב כיון שיצא השטר מתחת יד של המתחייב א"ו דעיקר הטעם לא לא מחמת זכי' דהא ממילא זכה רק כל זמן שהוא תחת ידו יש לו מגו אבל כיון שיצא מתחת ידו יהיה באיזה אופן עכ"פ ל"ל מגו וזוכה בו ולכך תלה הטעם דיצא מתחת ידו וזה ברור ומדוקדק בדברי הטור ולדעת הב"ח וש"ך עיקר חסר בדברי טור:
urim_vetumim_tumim.en: He acquired his share, etc. Shach attacks this ruling. Baal HaTerumot, Shaar 52, records a dispute. Even R. Natan bar Meir, who supports the rule that delivery to one creditor can operate for both, appears to say so only where the borrower did not expressly require the document to be placed in his own hands. If he said, "Give it specifically to me," then according to that view the second creditor should not acquire merely because the document reached the first creditor, unless the first was explicitly appointed to acquire for his colleague. Shach therefore says Mechaber's ruling is too broad. There is no difficulty against Mechaber. R. Natan bar Meir's entire discussion follows Rif's system, in which even after a kinyan the creditor's right does not fully arise until the document reaches him. If so, where the borrower says, "Give it to me," the second creditor plainly has not received what Rif requires. But we follow the later authorities who reject Rif and hold that an ordinary kinyan itself creates the creditor's substantive right without requiring physical delivery. On that view, once the kinyan was made, both creditors already acquired. The reason Mechaber speaks of the document being delivered to one of them is not because that delivery creates the second creditor's legal acquisition. It removes the borrower's evidentiary migo. So long as the document remains in the borrower's hands, he can destroy it or claim the obligation never became operative. Once the paper leaves his possession, that migo is gone. Then both creditors can enforce the rights they already acquired through the kinyan. This is why Mechaber's ruling is sound. Even if one accepts Rif's requirement of delivery, there is another analogy that supports Mechaber. A deathbed gift and a deed found tied to the deceased's body ordinarily require some act showing the donor intended the gift to take effect. Yet Mechaber rules below in siman 250, seif 25, that where one person gives gifts to many and effects acquisition for one beneficiary, that can confirm the entire testamentary arrangement. Sema explains that giving effect to one portion reveals a general intent that the whole gift stand. R. Natan bar Meir himself derives the present rule from the case of acquiring for one through another. Thus, even under a delivery-based model, delivery to one can sometimes confirm the entire multi-beneficiary obligation. Mechaber's ruling is therefore defensible from either direction. The greater difficulty is actually Tur. Tur seems, as explained above, to follow Rosh's position that in a loan kinyan physical delivery can still matter. If so, Shach's objection has more force against Tur: why should delivery to one creditor help the other? There is also a textual difficulty. Below in siman 250, Tur omits R. Natan bar Meir's explanation of the deathbed-gift rule and instead cites Rashbam and Raavad. If he did not adopt R. Natan bar Meir's mechanism there, why rely upon it here? The answer is that Tur's present case is not an ordinary future loan at all. He says the debtor "obligated himself to two people by kinyan." That language indicates a complete present obligation, like a gift, effective whether or not any later loan is advanced. The phrase "obligated himself" means a final undertaking, not merely a contemplated borrowing. Baal HaTerumot, the source of Tur's law, likewise discusses it in the framework of a gift-like absolute obligation. In such a shtar aknayata, as explained above, the borrower cannot retract the substantive obligation even before the paper reaches the creditor. Thus both creditors already acquired. Why then does Tur say, "Once the document left the obligor's possession, both acquired"? Because while the document remains in his own hands he retains an evidentiary migo, such as destroying the document or claiming the obligation was subject to a condition. Once it leaves his possession in any manner, that migo disappears. This is why Tur does not say, "Once the first creditor acquired, the second acquired through him." He says specifically, "Once the document left the obligor's possession." That wording proves the reason is not that the first creditor acts as an agent acquiring for the second. The underlying rights already existed. The only significance of the paper leaving the debtor is removal of his migo. Accordingly, Bach and Shach's explanation omits the main point. Tur's language is exact, and Mechaber's ruling is correct from every side.

urim_vetumim_urim.he: זכה בחלקו כו' עיין תומים שהעליתי דאפילו אין שותף בהחוב ואפילו נמסר ליד אחר זכה בו דקנין לא בעי מטי לידי' רק אם הוא תחת יד המתחייב וטוען תנאי היה בינינו שלא אתחייב לך קודם הלואה נאמן במגו דקלתי' או דהיה טוען פרעתי. אבל אם נתנו ליד אחר תו ל"ל מגו:
urim_vetumim_urim.en: He was given in part as a sign that I raised, Despite, there was no partner in the debt, and even delivered to another side, he received a succinctly to me only if he was under the hand of the pledge and claims a condition was between us that I would not compel you before a faithful loan in the palm or dehy claims I had broken. But if they were given a note to “Galm”:

mechaber.he: עדים שראו קטן שקנו מידו לא יכתבו עליו שטר:
mechaber.en: Witnesses who saw a small man who had bought from his hands would not write a note on him:

baer_hetev.he: שטר. כי הקנין שלו אינו כלום. ש"ך:
baer_hetev.en: bill. Because his canine is nothing. “Third:

beer_hagolah.he: ו) ב"י בשם הטור סימן צ"ו מסל"ב

netivot_hamishpat_hidushim.he: לא יכתבו. וה"ה אם אמר כתבו דאין קנין ושטר מקטן כלום:
netivot_hamishpat_hidushim.en: They will not write. “If he said, do not write a little bit of anything:

rabbi_akiva_eiger.he: [הגה] אבל אם אמר להלוות לו על משכון. באורי' כ' בשו"ת נזכר משכנות קרקע והרמ"א סתם משום דס"ל גם במטלטלי' וכו'. עיי"ש ולענ"ד דין זה צ"ע במטלטלי' במה נתחייב להלוות דהא לא זכה זה שעבוד במטלטלי' להפוסקי' דס"ל במנה אין כאן וכו' דהטעם דמשיכה לא מהני לקנות לשעבודו דלא מקרי משיכה כיון דהדרי' למרי'. עיין הר"ן רפ"ו דשבועות לענין משכון אם הוי כהילך. וצ"ע:
rabbi_akiva_eiger.en: [Rama] But if he said to lend to him upon collateral. Note: Urim writes that the responsum refers to a mortgage of land, and that the Rama stated the rule without qualification because he holds that it applies also to movable property. See there. In my humble opinion, the law requires study with respect to movable property. By what act did the prospective lender become obligated to lend? The other party did not acquire a lien in the movable property according to the authorities who hold, in the case of "there is no maneh here," that meshichah does not acquire the object for the purpose of a lien, because such pulling is not considered a true acquisition when the object must return to its owner. See the Ran at the beginning of the sixth chapter of Shevuot concerning whether collateral is considered "here it is." This requires study.

siftei_kohen.he: לא יכתבו עליו שטר כי הקנין שלו אינו כלום:
siftei_kohen.en: It will not be written because his canine is nothing:

turei_zahav.he: (בא"ד וע' בתשו' הרשב"א סי' אלף וקמ"ט וכו') ע"ש דמבואר דסובר דהלכתא כמר בר"א וע"ל סי' ס"א סעיף י"ז שהעתיק בתשובת הרשב"א דמשמע שם דאינו מצריך אלא דכנפינ' ולא מצריך שישלחו כמו דס"ל למר בר"א צ"ל דהתם איירי שהודה ע"י תביעה ומהני הודאה כמ"ש בשם הנ"י לעיל אבל בשו"ת דאלף וקמ"ט מיירי בהודה מעצמו וק"ל:
turei_zahav.en: (There: see Rashba, responsum 1149, etc.) Rashba there clearly rules like Mar bar Rav Ashi. Below, siman 61, seif 17, a Rashba responsum is cited implying that gathering the judges suffices and no summons is needed, unlike Mar bar Rav Ashi. That case must involve an admission made in response to a claim, which is effective as explained above in the name of the Nimukei Yosef. Responsum 1149 concerns a spontaneous admission.

urim_vetumim_urim.he: לא יכתבו עליו שטר וה"ה אם אמר כתבו דאין בשטר שלו וקנין שלו ממש אבל מלוה ע"פ הוי בדבר שמקחו מקח:
urim_vetumim_urim.en: It will not be written about him, and “If he says he does not write in his filter and his canon, but he is accompanied by what he is taking:

mechaber.he: עדים שראו דבר לזכות לראובן ואין זכותו נגמר עד שיביא עדים שראו עוד דבר אחר אם כותבין העדים ונותנים מה שראו בסימן ר"ה:
mechaber.en: Witnesses who have seen anything to win the victim and have no end until witnesses have seen anything else if they write the witnesses and give them what they saw in the letter:

rabbi_akiva_eiger.he: [ש"ך אות מט] עוד נחלקו גדולים. נ"ב באו"ת כ' להוכיח מבב"מ ע"ז דאם נותן לו שט"ח אינו קונה קרקע מדין כסף וממילא נפשט מיניה דהדין כהרשב"א. דלשיטת רמב"ן כמו דס' בשע"ק הוי כהקנה קרקע ה"נ הו"ל להיות קנין כמו החליף קרקע בקרקע. ולענ"ד מה דפשיטא לי' דלהרמב"ן יכול לקנות בזה קרקע בשט"ח. זהו נסתר מהרמב"ן פ"ק דקדושין בסוגי' מנה אין כאן וכו' דס"ל דהפירוש כיון דהעיקר הכסף עדיין גבי' והלה לא זכה רק השעבוד לא מקרי כסף עיי"ש וע"כ הא דס"ל דצריך הלוה להלות היינו דמ"מ כיון דקנה השעבוד מחוייב בדמיו. אולם לעומת זה גם מה דפשיטא לי' לאו"ת לדינא דאין לקנות קרקע בשט"ח ג"ז אינו לאידך שיטות דפ"ק דקדושין דלדידהו דהדין דהנותן שט"ח לאשה מתקדשת בו. עיי' ח"מ וב"ש אה"ע סי' כ"ט ה"נ ברור דקונה קרקע בכה"ג. כן נ"ל דעיקר דין זה תלוי במחלוקת הפוסקים אלו. אבל במחלוקת כאן אם הלוה צריך להלות אינו תלוי' בזה דאף אם אינו קונה קרקע דלא מקרי כסף קנין. מ"מ י"ל דנתחייב בדמיו וצריך להלותו. וכן אף אם קונה קרקע ע"י שט"ח י"ל דהתם זהו חליפי קנין דנותן הקרקע בשביל הדמים. אבל בהלואה אין הלוה נותן המעות בשביל השעבוד דהא רוצה בחזרת מעותיו ואינו רוצה לקנות במעותיו דבר מחבירו אלא דרוצה בשעבוד נכסי' להיות בטוח במעותיו. אבל אין הלוה מקנה לו דבר חליפי זה. אולם בגוף דברי הרשב"א בת' אלף נ"ד ששם מקור דין זה תמוה לי דמתחלה כתב להוכיח דא"צ להלוות לו מהא דכותבי' שטר ללוה וכו' דל"ח שיכריחו להלוות. א"כ מהך ראי' גופי' מוכח דס"ל דגם במקח אם המוכר כתב שטר מקח מדעת הלוקח דלא נתחייב זה בדמיו ואלו בדין משכנתא כתב הרשב"א שם דבהחזיק א"י לחזור המלוה ואם לא החזיק יכול לחזור וסיים ואם מפני הקנין וכו' ז"א דאפי' בשטר וקנין אינו קונה בלא כסף. עכ"ל משמע דמספקא לי' בדינא ואם במשכנתא א"י לחזור פשיטא דגם במקח א"י לחזור והו"ל להרשב"א להכריע כהך שיטה דבקנין אינו קונה בלא כסף מדכותבי' שטר למוכר דע"כ מיירי בקנין מדלא חיישינן דדלמא כ' ליתן בניסן עיי"ש וצ"ע:
rabbi_akiva_eiger.en: [Shach, letter 49] Further, leading authorities disagreed. Note: Urim seeks to prove from Bava Metzia 77 that if one gives another a promissory note, the recipient does not thereby acquire land by the acquisition of money, and from this he concludes that the law follows the Rashba. For according to the Ramban, just as a promissory note upon which one has a lien is viewed as transferring land, so too it should effect an acquisition like an exchange of land for land. In my humble opinion, Urim's premise that according to the Ramban one can acquire land by giving a promissory note is contradicted by the Ramban in the first chapter of Kiddushin, in the sugya of "there is no maneh here." The Ramban explains that since the principal money remains with the giver and the other party acquires only the lien, this is not considered money. See there. Necessarily, when the Ramban holds that the borrower must make the loan, the reason is that once the borrower acquired the lien he became obligated to pay its value. Conversely, Urim's assumption that as a matter of law one cannot acquire land with a promissory note is also not correct according to the other approaches in the first chapter of Kiddushin. According to those authorities, a woman who receives a promissory note in kiddushin is betrothed by it; see Chelkat Mechokek and Beit Shmuel, Even HaEzer, siman 29. It is therefore clear that, according to them, land can likewise be acquired in this manner. In my view, this particular question depends upon that dispute among the authorities. The dispute here, however, whether the lender must actually lend, does not necessarily depend upon it. Even if a promissory note cannot acquire land because it is not considered acquisition-money, one can still say that the borrower became liable for its value and therefore must lend him. Likewise, even if land can be acquired by a promissory note, that may be because in a sale the land is given in exchange for the money. In a loan, by contrast, the borrower is not giving the money in exchange for the lien, for the lender wants his money returned and does not intend to purchase anything from the borrower with it. He wants only the lien on the borrower's assets as security for repayment. Thus the borrower does not transfer anything to him as an exchange for the money. Yet the Rashba's own words in Responsa, siman 1054, which are the source of this law, are difficult to me. He first proves that the lender need not lend from the law that one may write a deed for the borrower, because we do not fear that the borrower will then compel the lender to lend. This very proof would imply that even in a sale, if the seller writes a deed of sale with the buyer's consent, the buyer has not thereby become obligated to pay. Yet regarding a mortgage the Rashba writes there that if the lender took possession he may not retract, while if he did not take possession he may retract. He concludes that a kinyan does not solve the problem, because even a deed with a kinyan does not acquire without money. This implies that the matter was doubtful to him. If with a mortgage the lender cannot retract after possession, then certainly in a sale the buyer cannot retract. The Rashba should therefore have resolved the dispute in favor of the view that a kinyan without money does not acquire, based on the rule that a deed may be written for the seller, which necessarily speaks of a case with a kinyan, since otherwise we would fear that he wrote it in order to give it only later. See there. This requires study.

turei_zahav.he: (ע"ש בד"א שאין כותבין וכו' עד והם כדברי הרמב"ם בפ"ז מטוען ונטען וכו') אינו מוכרח בדבריהם כיון שהם מחוסרים גוביינא ויכול לתבעו פעם שנית ויצטרך לשלם בהלואה כיון שיהי' לו שטר עליו מה שא"כ בפקדון דאף שיהיה לו שטר עליו ולא יוכל לתבעו שנית דיהי' נאמן בהחזרתו במגו דנאנסו אף בשטר ובהדיא כ' הרמב"ם הטעם במטלטלי דיוכל לתבעו שנית וכן משמע קצת במ"מ דלא כתב הרמב"ם גבי מטלטלי לאפוקי מרבוותא דס"ל אף בהלוואה מטלטלי בעינייהו כותבין אבל לא בא לשלול פקדון דלא שייך ביה דתבעו שנית ודוק אבל הרשב"א בתשובה סימן א' רי"א סובר כדעת הנ"י וצריך לדחוק בפי' הגמרא לדעת':
turei_zahav.en: (See there: when does this rule that they do not write apply, etc., until: and these are the words of Rambam in chapter 7 of Hilchot To'en VeNitan, etc.) This is not compelled by their words. Since movable property still requires actual collection and the creditor could sue the borrower again and force him to pay a second time if he held a document, Rambam's reason applies to a loan. By contrast, in the case of a deposit, even if the depositor has a document, he cannot necessarily sue a second time, because the custodian is believed to say that he returned it through a migo that it was lost through unavoidable circumstances, even against a document. Rambam explicitly gives as the reason regarding movable property that the creditor could sue a second time, and the Maggid Mishneh also somewhat implies that Rambam did not write this merely to exclude authorities who hold that even with a loan involving identifiable movable property a document may be written. He did not necessarily intend to exclude a deposit, where the concern of a second claim does not apply. Examine carefully. Rashba, however, in responsum 111, agrees with the Nimukei Yosef's position, and one must therefore interpret the Gemara somewhat forcefully according to that view.

mechaber.he: לוה שבא לב"ד בשטר חוב שבידו לכפות את המלוה להלותו עד זמן שקבע אפי' נתברר שמדעת המלוה נכתב יכול לחזור בו (אבל אם אמר להלוות לו על משכון והחזיק במשכון לא יוכל לחזור בו) (תשובת רשב"א סי' אלף נ"ד) הלוה נותן שכר הסופר אפילו הוא שטר עיסקא ואם המלוה אבד השטר וצריך לכתוב אחר הוא נותן השכר (נ"י פ' גט פשוט והמגיד פכ"ד מה' מלוה):
mechaber.en: A borrower who comes to beit din holding a promissory note and seeks to compel the lender to lend him the money until the term stated in the document cannot compel him, even if it is established that the document was written with the lender's consent, because the lender may retract. <small>However, if he agreed to lend against collateral and took possession of the collateral, he may no longer retract.</small> The borrower pays the scribe's fee, even when the document is an iska agreement. <small>If the lender lost the document and a replacement must be written, the lender pays the fee.</small>

baer_hetev.he:
לחזור. ז"ל הע"ש ונרא' שצריך להחזיר לו שכר הסופר שנתן מדיני דגרמי ע"ש ודברי טעם הן עכ"ל סמ"ע וכתב הש"ך דהר"י ן' מיג"ש והרמב"ן חולקים על דין זה והמחבר הביא דבריהם בס"ס רל"ח. וק"ק למה סתם כאן ונרא' דדין זה הוי ספיקא דדינא והמוחזק יוכל לומר קים לי כהרמב"ן וסייעתו וכ"כ בתשובת מבי"ט ח"א סי' ר' וסי' רי"ג ע"ש. עוד נחלקו גדולים עם המבי"ט שם במי שמכר צמר לחבירו וכתב לו שטר על סך דמי המכיר' ומת הלה שלקחו ותפס ב"ח של הלוקח הצמר מרשות המוכר שכתב המבי"ט דאפילו הרשב"א מודה במטלטלים והחולקים כתבו דאפילו הרמב"ן מודה במטלטלים ע"ש באריכות ונ"ל כהחולקין וא"כ אותו ב"ח של הלוקח שלא כדין תפס עוד נרא' עיקר דכשמת הלו' יכול המלו' לחזור בו אף להרמב"ן וכן כשנודע בינתים שיגיע להמלו' איזה הפסד מזה כגון שלא יהי' בטוח במעותיו וכה"ג ומן הסברא נרא' כן דמסתמא אדעתא דהכי לא נתרצ' זה כו' ע"ש וכתב עוד בשם מ"ב דאפילו בא השטר ליד המלו' כ"ז שלא נתן המעות יכול לחזור כו' וע' בטור וב"י עכ"ל:
עיסקא. מחצי הריוח יתן ליד המלו' אפ"ה צריך המקבל ליתן כל שכר הכתיב'. סמ"ע:
נותן. כ"כ בד"מ בשם נ"י ושכן משמע בהרב המגיד ובאמת ליתא כן בנ"י ובה"ה דשם קאי אשובר כו' מיהו דין זה אמת מסברא וע"ל סי' נ"ד ס"א עכ"ל הש"ך:
baer_hetev.en:
To retract. The Ir Shushan writes that it appears he must reimburse the other party for the scribe's fee that was paid, under the laws of causative damages. The Sema says that this reasoning is sound. The Shach writes that Ri Migash and the Ramban disagree with this law, and the Mechaber cites their views at the end of siman 238. It is therefore difficult that the Mechaber rules categorically here. It appears that the matter is a doubt in law, and the possessor may say, "I rely on the Ramban and those who agree with him." Responsa Mabit, part 1, simanim 200 and 213, states likewise. Great authorities also disputed with the Mabit concerning a person who sold wool to another and wrote him a note for the price. The purchaser died, and a creditor of the purchaser seized the wool from the seller's possession. The Mabit wrote that even the Rashba would agree with regard to movable property, while those who disagreed held that even the Ramban would agree with regard to movable property. See there at length. The Shach concludes that the dissenters are correct, and therefore the purchaser's creditor seized unlawfully.
